name: Whitening powder (charcoal)
lead: Charcoal whitening powder is activated charcoal sold as a fine black powder that people brush onto their teeth to lift surface stain from coffee, tea and similar sources. The aim is a brighter-looking smile, and charcoal powders sit alongside strips, pens, rinses and whitening toothpastes among consumer whitening formats.[1][2]

Proponents say the charcoal adsorbs pigments and works as a mild abrasive, so stained enamel looks lighter after brushing. A British Dental Journal review describes charcoal toothpastes and powders as fashionable products used for tooth brushing, extrinsic stain removal and, as claimed, whitening, and notes that dental teams are often asked about them and answer largely from experience rather than trial data.[2]

Research is small but exists. A 2024 randomized clinical trial compared charcoal powder and charcoal toothpaste with regular fluoride toothpaste and 10% carbamide peroxide; the charcoal products produced whitening comparable to regular toothpaste, with carbamide peroxide giving the largest change.[3]

Charcoal powders belong to a wider family of home whitening formats that also includes peroxide strips, gels, rinses and whitening toothpastes. Wikipedia reports that whitening toothpastes lighten teeth by one or two shades with continued use, mainly through added abrasives and detergents, while peroxide products change color through bleaching [1].

chain: Charcoal adsorbs and abrades surface stain
angle.text: The goal is removing extrinsic stain from the enamel surface so teeth look cleaner and lighter. It acts on surface discoloration rather than on color inside the tooth, which is what peroxide products target.

paras: Users usually apply the powder with a wet toothbrush or fingertip. Wikipedia notes that whitening toothpastes in general contain more abrasives and detergents than regular pastes to help remove stain, while peroxide-based products change tooth color by bleaching.[1]
Charcoal products are marketed in powder, toothpaste and mouthwash forms in many countries, including the UK, US, Japan, India, Thailand, Australia, Hong Kong, China and Korea.[2]

On looksmax.org, a thread asks whether charcoal can clean teeth; one reply suggests whitening strips instead because they are faster, and another says charcoal is corrosive and can wear enamel if used often.[4]

A 2020 in vitro study stained forty human canines with coffee and compared brushing with deionised water, regular toothpaste and charcoal-containing products over a simulated 90 days for color change and enamel surface alteration.[5]

A 2023 randomized laboratory trial brushed aged resin composite specimens with a charcoal dentifrice or whitening toothpastes for 14 minutes. Surface roughness did not differ significantly between groups, though roughness rose after brushing within each group.[6]

Activated carbon, also called activated charcoal, is carbon processed to develop many tiny pores, giving a very large surface area, in some cases above 3,000 square metres per gram. It binds substances by adsorption, where molecules stick to a surface, rather than absorption.[8] It is widely used to filter water and air and is also used medically after oral poisoning, and the encyclopedia lists teeth whitening among its many applications.[8]

sections.h: How it is meant to work
paras: The reasoning given by proponents is that activated charcoal is a highly porous material that binds pigment molecules, and that its fine gritty particles lift surface stain mechanically when brushed. This targets extrinsic stain from foods, drinks and tobacco. Wikipedia describes the same split in general whitening products: abrasives and detergents help remove extrinsic stain, whereas peroxide acts on intrinsic stain by releasing free radicals that break pigment molecules into smaller, less pigmented fragments [1].

Because charcoal contains no peroxide, it is not expected to change the colour inside the tooth. The 2019 British Dental Journal review characterises the products as marketed for brushing, stain removal and whitening, with dental teams answering patient questions largely from experience [2].

In Wikipedia's overview, strips are applied twice daily for 30 minutes over 14 days and were introduced in the late 1980s, gels are brushed on twice daily for 14 days, rinses are used for one minute twice daily with visible results sometimes taking up to three months, and carbamide peroxide trays can show results within days [1]. The US FDA is described as accepting gels under 6% hydrogen peroxide or up to 16% carbamide peroxide [1]. In the EU, retail products are limited to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide and higher concentrations may be supplied only by dental professionals [1]. Charcoal products are generally sold as cosmetics or toothpastes and contain no peroxide.

Wikipedia also says that excessively abrasive whitening pastes can harm dental tissue, and it presents baking soda as a lower-abrasion alternative [1]. Sensitivity is described as the most common side effect of peroxide whitening, with 67 to 78 percent of in-office patients reporting it [1].

A 2014 narrative update by Clifton Carey in the Journal of Evidence-Based Dental Practice describes peroxide-based whitening as safe and effective when manufacturer instructions are followed, with tooth sensitivity and gum irritation the most common side effects.[7] It also reports laboratory findings of enamel softening and roughening with aggressive, high-concentration treatments, and that home bleaching causes less sensitivity than in-office bleaching with comparable results over time.[7]
The same review notes that whitening lasts longer when teeth avoid staining agents such as coffee, red wine and tobacco, the same extrinsic stains charcoal powders are marketed to remove.[7]

Efforts to whiten teeth date back centuries: Wikipedia mentions Roman dentists using urine mixed with goat milk, barbers in the late 1600s filing teeth and applying acid, and oxalic acid in 1877, followed by calcium hypochlorite [1]. Custom-tray bleaching with carbamide peroxide was introduced by Dr William Klusmeier in the late 1960s, and consumer strips followed in the late 1980s [1]. The British Dental Journal review describes charcoal toothpastes and powders as fashionable products [2].

The enamel question is the main safety discussion. The 2020 laboratory study evaluated enamel colour change and surface morphology after brushing with charcoal-containing paste and mouthwash [5], and the 2023 study found no significant difference in roughness of aged resin composite between charcoal and whitening toothpastes, though roughness rose within every group after brushing [6]. The BDJ review notes that strong evidence behind manufacturers' claims is lacking [2]. Product abrasivity varies by formulation.

A single-blind randomized trial in 56 volunteers (four groups of 14, 14 days of treatment) compared activated charcoal powder, charcoal toothpaste, fluoride toothpaste and 10% carbamide peroxide. Charcoal products whitened to a degree similar to regular toothpaste; carbamide peroxide gave the best result and highest satisfaction. The authors called the charcoal effect minor and unsatisfactory.[3] Beyond this trial, published clinical data on charcoal powders are limited, and the 2019 review noted the lack of strong evidence behind manufacturers' claims.[2]

lore.intro: Charcoal powder is discussed on looksmax.org as a home alternative to whitening strips, with members raising questions about whether it works and whether it abrades enamel.[4]

claims.claim: Charcoal lifts stain and whitens teeth
claims.believers: Proponents say black charcoal binds stain and brightens teeth when brushed on.[2]
claims.experts: A 2024 randomized trial found charcoal powder whitened about as much as regular fluoride toothpaste, with carbamide peroxide giving a larger effect.[3]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply says it is corrosive and can strip enamel if used often, and another advises strips instead.[4]
claims.experts: Laboratory studies have examined enamel and composite surface effects of charcoal products; one found no significant roughness differences between charcoal and other whitening toothpastes.[5][6]

claims.claim: Whitening strips work faster than charcoal
claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply recommends strips because they are faster.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes peroxide strips as used over about 14 days and carbamide peroxide trays as showing results within days, while the 2024 trial found carbamide peroxide whitened more than charcoal products.[1][3]

claims.claim: Charcoal works because it adsorbs pigment
claims.believers: Proponents say charcoal's porous structure binds stain molecules.[2]
claims.experts: Activated carbon is a strongly adsorbing material in general, and the 2019 BDJ review assessed how strong the evidence is for manufacturers' whitening claims, reporting it as lacking.[2][8]

card.summary: Brush-on activated charcoal powder for surface stain; only lab research exists.

quick.overview:
Charcoal whitening powder is brushed onto teeth in the hope of removing surface stain.

Only a laboratory study of a related charcoal product was identified; no human trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say the charcoal adsorbs and abrades stain from enamel. It does not bleach internal tooth colour.
quick.risks: General whitening toothpastes contain abrasives; the effect of charcoal on enamel has been examined in vitro. No clinical safety data were found.
